mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: the agents in the instrumental (शुम्भनिशुम्भाभ्याम् असुराभ्याम्), the things seized in the nominative (त्रैलोक्यम् यज्ञभागाः च), the cause in the ablative (मदबलाश्रयात्).
mantras.lit: Formerly, by the two asuras Śumbha and Niśumbha, through reliance on (their) pride and strength, the three worlds and the sacrificial shares of Śacī’s lord were taken away.
mantras.tr: Long ago the asuras Śumbha and Niśumbha, trusting in their pride and their strength, seized from Indra, Śacī’s lord, the three worlds and his share of the sacrifices.
mantras.tr_note: The passive is turned into an active sentence; ‘from Indra’ renders the genitive शचीपतेः.

comm.t: Medhas opens the third story with a usurpation, as he opened the second (2.2–3): the demons take Indra’s rule over the three worlds and the gods’ shares of the sacrifice. This time the enemies are two brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha, and their strength is said to rest on pride (मद).

In the Gita Press pāṭha the Uttama Carita has its own viniyoga: Rudra is its ṛṣi, Mahāsarasvatī its devatā, anuṣṭubh its metre; its dhyāna pictures Mahāsarasvatī as born from the body of Gaurī and as the destroyer of Śumbha and the other daityas. This assignment is liturgical tradition, not part of the Purāṇa’s narrative.

The abstract suffix -tā (tal) makes a feminine noun of state from सूर्य: ‘Sun-ness’, i.e. the Sun’s function.
Taddhita with vṛddhi of the first vowel (इ → ऐ) and guṇa of the final u (u → av): इन्दु → ऐन्दव ‘belonging to the Moon’. कौबेर and याम्य are formed the same way from कुबेर and यम.

mantras.anvaya: तौ एव सूर्यताम्, तद्वत् ऐन्दवम् अधिकारम्, तथा कौबेरम् अथ याम्यम् वरुणस्य च (अधिकारम्) चक्राते।
mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (चक्राते) with a list of objects: the Sun’s state, and the offices of the Moon, Kubera, Yama and Varuṇa; अधिकारम् is understood with each adjective, and वरुणस्य is a genitive standing for a fifth.
mantras.lit: Those two themselves took over the state of the Sun, likewise the office of the Moon, so too that of Kubera, and of Yama, and of Varuṇa.
mantras.tr: They seized for themselves the Sun’s place, and in the same way the offices of the Moon, of Kubera, of Yama and of Varuṇa.

comm.t: The brothers do not merely defeat the gods; they take over their functions in the cosmos one by one: the Sun, the Moon, Kubera (wealth), Yama (death) and Varuṇa (the waters).

The list repeats the complaint of the gods against Mahiṣa in 2.6 (सूर्येन्द्राग्न्यनिलेन्दूनां यमस्य वरुणस्य च … अधिकारान्). Each carita begins with the order of the worlds overturned; the Goddess appears to restore it.

mantras.anvaya: तौ एव पवनर्द्धिम् च वह्निकर्म च चक्रतुः। ततः देवाः पराजिताः भ्रष्टराज्याः विनिर्धूताः (अभवन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the list of 5.3 with a new verb; the second is a nominal sentence of three participles with देवाः as subject.
mantras.lit: Those two themselves took over the might of the Wind and the work of Fire. Then the gods, defeated, their kingdom lost, were driven out.
mantras.tr: They took the Wind’s power too, and the office of Fire. So the gods, defeated and stripped of their kingdom, were cast out.

comm.t: The usurpation is complete: Wind and Fire follow Sun, Moon, Kubera, Yama and Varuṇa. The second line gives the result in three participles: defeated, kingdomless, expelled.
Fire (वह्नि) carries the offerings to the gods; its work in demon hands means the sacrifice itself no longer reaches them, which completes the loss of the यज्ञभागाः named in 5.2.

mantras.lit: Deprived of their offices, all the Thirty, cast out by those two great asuras, call to mind that Goddess, the Unconquered.
mantras.tr: Robbed of their offices and driven out by the two great asuras, all the gods turned their minds to that Goddess, the Unconquered One.
mantras.tr_note: The historic present संस्मरन्ति is rendered as a past.

comm.t: The gods do not fight back; they remember. The verb सं-√स्मृ prepares the next verse, where the boon they recall was given precisely for remembrance. The Goddess is called Aparājitā, ‘unconquered’, in the verse after the gods were called पराजिताः, ‘conquered’.

The remembrance answers the end of the fourth chapter: there the gods asked that whenever she was remembered she would destroy their calamities (4.35–36), and she consented (4.39). The third story begins by invoking that promise.

the gravest misfortunes; the first member stands in its stem form परम-

morph.note: Simple future of the causative stem नाशय- (√नश् ‘perish’ → ‘cause to perish’) with the future marker -इष्य-: नाशय् + इष्य + आमि.
A feminine participle with the force of a condition: ‘(I,) being remembered’, i.e. ‘whenever I am remembered’. The Goddess is quoted speaking of herself.
Genitive for the recipient: वरः अस्माकं दत्तः, ‘a boon was given of us’ = ‘to us’, a common use of the genitive in place of the dative.

mantras.anvaya: तया अस्माकम् वरः दत्तः, यथा — आपत्सु स्मृता (अहम्) भवताम् अखिलाः परमापदः तत्क्षणात् नाशयिष्यामि (इति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive main clause (तया … वरः दत्तः) followed by the boon in direct speech, introduced by यथा: the Goddess is the unexpressed subject of नाशयिष्यामि, and स्मृता is a participle of condition.
mantras.lit: By her a boon was given to us, that: ‘Remembered in calamities, I shall at that very moment destroy all your extreme calamities.’
mantras.tr: She gave us a boon: ‘When I am remembered in your misfortunes, I will that very instant destroy all your direst calamities.’
mantras.tr_note: The verse is the gods’ own thought, closed by इति in 5.7; the passive ‘was given by her’ is rendered as active.

comm.t: The gods recall the promise made at the end of the second story: they asked, संस्मृता संस्मृता त्वं नो हिंसेथाः परमापदः (4.36), and she consented (4.39). Here the same promise is quoted in her own voice, with the same word परमापदः.
A modern reading: the gods have lost everything except a promise, and their first act is to remember it. In this text remembrance is not a feeling but the condition on which help arrives.

samasa.sense: the Himālaya, king of mountains
the Goddess as the māyā belonging to Viṣṇu (compare Hari’s Mahāmāyā, 1.55); the name returns in the first yā devī stanza (5.14–16)

morph.note: Perfect of √स्तु: the reduplicating syllable keeps the stop (तु-, not स्तु-), and the root’s s becomes ṣ after u (तुष्टु-); before the ending -उः the u becomes uv. With प्र: ‘they praised forth’.
Perfect of √गम्: reduplication ज- (g → j) and loss of the root vowel before the weak ending: ज-ग्म्-उः.
Absolutive: ‘having made (up their) mind’; the action precedes that of the main verb जग्मुः.

mantras.anvaya: इति मतिम् कृत्वा देवाः नगेश्वरम् हिमवन्तम् जग्मुः। ततः तत्र विष्णुमायाम् देवीम् प्रतुष्टुवुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two main verbs with one subject (देवाः): जग्मुः with its goal हिमवन्तम्, and प्रतुष्टुवुः with its object देवीम्; कृत्वा marks the prior resolve.
mantras.lit: Having made up their mind thus, the gods went to Himavat, lord of mountains; there, then, they praised the Goddess Viṣṇumāyā.
mantras.tr: Resolved on this, the gods went to the Himālaya, king of mountains, and there they sang the praises of the Goddess, Viṣṇumāyā.

comm.t: The gods go to the Himālaya and begin the hymn that runs from 5.9 to 5.82. The place matters to the story: it is there that Pārvatī comes to bathe (5.84) and that Ambikā comes forth from her body (5.85–87).
The name Viṣṇumāyā links this hymn to the first story, where the Goddess was Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā and Mahāmāyā (1.54–55). The hymn’s first yā devī stanza names her by this very title (5.14–16).

mantras.anvaya: देव्यै नमः, महादेव्यै शिवायै सततम् नमः। प्रकृत्यै भद्रायै नमः। नियताः (वयम्) ताम् प्रणताः स्म।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three salutations with नमः and the dative, then a statement of the speakers: (वयम्) नियताः ताम् प्रणताः स्म ‘we, restrained, are bowed to her’.
mantras.lit: Salutation to the Goddess, to the Great Goddess; to Śivā always salutation. Salutation to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā. Self-restrained, we have bowed to her.
mantras.tr: Homage to the Goddess, to the Great Goddess; to the Auspicious One, homage for ever. Homage to Nature, the Primal One, to the Gracious One. With minds held still we bow before her.
mantras.tr_note: ‘The Primal One’ makes explicit that प्रकृति here is the cosmic principle, not ‘nature’ in the everyday sense.

comm.t: The gods’ hymn opens with salutations in the dative: the Goddess is named as Devī, Mahādevī, Śivā (the auspicious), Prakṛti (the source of the manifest world) and Bhadrā (the benign). The last pāda turns from address to statement: the gods describe themselves as restrained and bowed.
The hymn of 5.9–82 is recited on its own in the Śākta tradition as the Tantrokta Devīsūkta. Its opening verse is among the most widely recited in the text.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the names 209, महादेवी, and 53, शिवा, and the related 397, मूलप्रकृतिः. The shared epithets belong to a common Śākta vocabulary; the two works are separate.

flags.uncertain: स्म: the printed short form is required by the metre (the seventh syllable of an even anuṣṭubh pāda must be light, which स्मः before ताम् would not be). It is taken as the particle स्म with the copula understood; it is also commonly explained as standing for स्मः ‘we are’ with the visarga lost metri causa. The sense, ‘we bow to her’, is the same either way.

mantras.anvaya: रौद्रायै नमः। नित्यायै गौर्यै धात्र्यै नमः नमः। ज्योत्स्नायै इन्दुरूपिण्यै च सुखायै सततम् नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A series of datives, each group closed by नमः; च joins ज्योत्स्नायै and इन्दुरूपिण्यै.
mantras.lit: To the Fierce One salutation; to the Eternal, to Gaurī, to the Supporter salutation, salutation. To Moonlight, and to her whose form is the Moon, to Happiness, always salutation.
mantras.tr: Homage to the Fierce One; homage and homage to the Eternal, to Gaurī, to her who upholds all. To the Moonlight, to her whose form is the Moon, to Joy itself, homage for ever.
mantras.tr_note: ‘All’ is supplied with ‘upholds’; the Sanskrit has the bare agent noun धात्री.

comm.t: The hymn sets terrible and gentle names side by side: Raudrā, of Rudra’s fierceness, beside the cool Moon and its light, and Sukhā, happiness. The pairing is stated outright in 5.13 (अतिसौम्यातिरौद्रा). Gaurī, ‘the Fair’, is Pārvatī’s name; the story will soon show the bright Ambikā coming forth from Pārvatī and Pārvatī herself turning dark (5.85–88).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 136, नित्या, and 635, गौरी, and the related 935, जगद्धात्री. The names are shared epithets of the Goddess; the hymns are separate.

The regular genitive plural of प्रणत is प्रणतानाम्; the short form is explained either as a shortened (ārṣa) form of it, or from a root-noun stem प्रणत्. An accusative singular feminine does not fit the series of datives.
Present of √कृ, first person plural: the weak stem कुरु- loses its u before m (कुर्मः). नमः कुर्मः ‘we make obeisance’.
Enclitic dative of the second person. Up to here the gods spoke of the Goddess in the third person; ते is the first direct address in the hymn.

mantras.anvaya: कल्याण्यै प्रणताम् वृद्ध्यै सिद्ध्यै (च) नमः नमः कुर्मः। नैर्ऋत्यै भूभृताम् लक्ष्म्यै शर्वाण्यै ते नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line has a verb (कुर्मः ‘we make’) with नमः as its object and three datives; प्रणताम् qualifies वृद्ध्यै and सिद्ध्यै. The second line is verbless; ते sums up the three datives before it.
mantras.lit: To the Auspicious One, to the prosperity and the success of those who bow, we make salutation, salutation. To Nairṛtī, to the fortune of kings, to Śarvāṇī — to you salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Auspicious One, who is the increase and the fulfilment of all who bow to her, we offer homage and homage. To Nairṛtī, to the royal fortune of kings, to Śarvāṇī — to you, homage and homage.
mantras.tr_note: प्रणताम् is taken with वृद्ध्यै and सिद्ध्यै; it could also be taken with कल्याण्यै (‘to her who is the welfare of those who bow’).

comm.t: The gods name opposed aspects together. She is the welfare, increase and fulfilment of those who bow; she is also Nairṛtī, the power of Nirṛti, the deity of decay and misfortune and guardian of the south-west; she is the fortune of kings, and Śarvāṇī, wife of Śiva. With ते the hymn turns to address her directly.

One traditional gloss takes नैर्ऋती as the fortune of the rākṣasas (Nirṛti being their lord), set against the fortune of kings in the same line: she is the prosperity of both. The orthography नैर्ऋत्यै is the Gita Press’s; GRETIL and Freund print नैरृत्यै, the same word.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 324, कल्याणी, and 124, शर्वाणी. Shared names, separate works.

flags.uncertain: प्रणताम्: a short genitive plural (for प्रणतानाम्), taken with वृद्ध्यै and सिद्ध्यै; its exact derivation is uncertain (ārṣa shortening, or a root-noun प्रणत्). Variant (orthographic): नैर्ऋत्यै (Gita Press, kept) / नैरृत्यै (GRETIL, Freund).

samasa.literal: she by whom the far side of what is hard to cross (is reached)
samasa.sense: she who carries her devotees across every difficulty
samasa.alt: Also read as a kṛt formation from the causative पारय- ‘to bring across’: दुर्गं पारयति इति दुर्गपारा, ‘she who brings (one) across difficulty’. The sense is the same.

samasa.sense: the Goddess as the agent of everything that is done

morph.note: कारिन् is √कृ with the kṛt affix ṇini (vṛddhi: कृ → कार्), ‘doer’; feminine कारिणी (n → ṇ after r in the same word).

दुर्ग ‘hard to go to, a fortress, a difficulty’ (दुस् + √गम्); as a name, दुर्गा is the Goddess who is hard to approach. The next word explains the name by its other sense: she is the crossing of difficulty.

mantras.anvaya: दुर्गायै दुर्गपारायै सारायै सर्वकारिण्यै ख्यात्यै तथा एव कृष्णायै धूम्रायै सततम् नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Eight datives, all governed by the one closing नमः.
mantras.lit: To Durgā, to her who is the far shore of difficulty, to the Essence, to the Maker of all, to Renown, and likewise to the Dark One, to the Smoke-hued One, always salutation.
mantras.tr: To Durgā, who brings us across every hardship; to the Essence, the Maker of all; to Renown, to the Dark One, to the Smoke-hued: homage for ever.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Brings us across every hardship’ renders the compound दुर्गपारा; ‘us’ is supplied.

comm.t: Durgā is explained by the next word: दुर्ग is what is hard to pass, and she is its far shore. The hymn of the second story said the same (दुर्गासि दुर्गभवसागरनौरसङ्गा, 4.11), and the battle will call her दुर्गा दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी (9.31). The dark and smoky names (कृष्णा, धूम्रा) anticipate 5.88, where Pārvatī becomes dark (कृष्णाभूत्) and is called Kālikā.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 190, दुर्गा. The name is common to Śākta hymns; the two texts are distinct.

samasa.alt: Not a dvandva: the two adjectives describe one and the same person, which is the karmadhāraya relation.

samasa.sense: she on whom the world rests

Dative of the i-stem कृति ‘doing, action’ (√कृ + ktin), with the feminine ending -ai. Not from कृत्या, whose dative would be कृत्यायै.

mantras.anvaya: अतिसौम्यातिरौद्रायै तस्यै नताः (वयम्) नमः नमः (कुर्मः)। जगत्प्रतिष्ठायै देव्यै कृत्यै नमः, नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line has the participle नताः for the speakers and the dative तस्यै with its long epithet; the second is a string of datives with नमः.
mantras.lit: Bowed, (we say) salutation, salutation to her who is most gentle and most fierce. Salutation to the foundation of the world, to the Goddess, to Action: salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: Bowing, we offer homage and homage to her who is at once most gentle and most terrible. Homage to the ground on which the world stands, to the Goddess, to Action itself: homage, homage.

comm.t: The verse states the paradox the earlier names had set side by side (रौद्रा and इन्दुरूपिणी, 5.10): she is both supremely gentle and supremely fierce. She is also the world’s foundation and action itself (कृति).

The tradition reads the same pairing in the story that follows: the beautiful Ambikā who dazzles the asuras’ servants (5.89–92) and the terrible Kālī who springs from her brow in the battle (chapter 7) are one Goddess. Praise and narrative tell one thing twice.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु विष्णुमाया इति शब्दिता, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः नमः (अस्तु)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या देवी … शब्दिता) and its correlative in the dative (तस्यै), governed by the repeated नमः. The pattern is the same in every yā devī stanza.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who in all beings is called ‘Viṣṇumāyā’ — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who in all beings is named Viṣṇu’s Māyā: homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.

comm.t: The first of the yā devī stanzas, the most recited part of the hymn. Each names one form under which the Goddess is present in every being and answers it with a threefold salutation. The series opens with the name the gods used when they began (विष्णुमाया, 5.7), and its first verb, शब्दिता, is about naming: she is what she is called in all beings.

In the Gita Press count each नमस्तस्यै is a separate mantra, so each yā devī stanza is three mantras; the chapter’s colophon counts 66 such mantras, 22 stanzas (5.14–76 and 5.78–80). The Goddess was first named Viṣṇu’s power in chapter 1, as the Yoganidrā that holds Viṣṇu and the Mahāmāyā of Hari (1.54–55).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name, 339, विष्णुमाया. The shared title is part of a common Śākta vocabulary; the texts are separate.

morph.note: Passive present of अभि + √धा: before the passive -ya- the root’s ā becomes ī (धीयते). अभि-√धा ‘to name’, passive ‘is called’.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु चेतना इति अभिधीयते, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः नमः (अस्तु)।

mantras.lit: The Goddess who in all beings is called ‘consciousness’ — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who in all beings is called Consciousness: homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.

comm.t: The second stanza moves from a title to what makes a being a being at all: awareness. Like the first it is a stanza of naming (अभिधीयते, ‘is called’); from the next stanza on the verb is संस्थिता and the formula …रूपेण, ‘abides in the form of’.
The series ends where this stanza begins, with consciousness: in 5.78–80 she is the one who, in the form of citi (चितिरूपेण), pervades the whole world.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 417, चेतनारूपा, ‘whose form is consciousness’, and 362, चितिः. The idea is shared; the works are distinct.

comm.t: The formula that carries the rest of the series appears here: …रूपेण संस्थिता, ‘abides in the form of …’. The first such form is बुद्धि, the understanding that discerns and decides.

The Devī Māhātmya returns to the line itself in the Nārāyaṇī hymn: सर्वस्य बुद्धिरूपेण जनस्य हृदि संस्थिते (11.8). Brahmā’s hymn had already called her बुद्धिः, ‘intelligence, whose mark is awakening’ (1.79).

comm.t: After intelligence, sleep: the state in which understanding is withdrawn is also a form of the Goddess. The series does not praise only what is noble; it finds her in every condition of a living being.
The name recalls the first story, where the Goddess is Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā, the sleep that holds the god until she withdraws (1.54, 1.69–71). Here the same power is present as sleep in all beings.

comm.t: Hunger, a want rather than a virtue, is named as her form. The series is deliberately inclusive: after intelligence and sleep come hunger, shadow and power, and later thirst (5.35–37) and even error (5.74–76). In chapter 1 hunger already belonged to Mahāmāyā’s work: birds, though tormented by hunger (पीड्यमानानपि क्षुधा), feed their young out of delusion (1.51–52).
A modern reading: to bow to the Goddess as hunger is to refuse to divide life into a sacred part and a merely bodily part. The need that drives every creature is itself where she is met.

comm.t: छाया is shadow and shade: the cool shelter from heat and the dark likeness that follows every body; the word can also mean a reflection. The text does not say which sense is meant, and the stanza names the form without explaining it.

comm.t: Śakti is the power or capacity by which anything acts at all. It is also the word the Śākta tradition uses for the Goddess herself, so this stanza names her by her most general name: she is the power in every being.
Brahmā’s hymn in chapter 1 said the same: ‘whatever is the power of all that exists, that is you’ (तस्य सर्वस्य या शक्तिः सा त्वम्, 1.83). The Nārāyaṇī hymn calls her वैष्णवी शक्तिः (11.5).

samasa.literal: by the form that is thirst

samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, तृष्णायाः रूपम् ‘the form of thirst’. The karmadhāraya fits better: the Goddess is not said to own a form belonging to thirst but to be present as thirst itself.

morph.note: तृष्णा is a feminine noun from √तृष् ‘to be thirsty’ (divādi, 4P, तृष्यति) with the suffix -na and feminine -ā: bodily thirst first, and by extension craving, longing for what one lacks.

Past passive participle of सम् + √स्था: the root’s ā becomes i before the -त of the participle (स्थित). With अस्ति understood it is the finite verb of the relative clause, ‘(who) abides, stands established’; feminine to agree with या देवी.

Instrumental singular of रूप in -एन; the n becomes ṇ because of the r earlier in the same word (internal retroflexion, which carries across vowels and labials). It is the instrumental of manner: ‘in the form of’.

Neuter s-stem नमस् ‘bowing, homage’, nominative singular. The one honoured stands in the dative (तस्यै); the verb (अस्तु) is not expressed. Each of the first two नमस्तस्यै is counted as a mantra of its own; the third, with नमो नमः, closes the three-part mantra.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु तृष्णारूपेण संस्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … संस्थिता) with its correlative तस्यै; each नमः takes the dative. The second line is three mantras in the pāṭha: नमस्तस्यै, नमस्तस्यै, and नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of thirst — homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as thirst: salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her — salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘As’ renders the instrumental -रूपेण ‘in the form of’; ‘again and again’ renders the doubled नमो नमः.

comm.t: The gods name the Goddess as thirst (तृष्णा) present in every creature. In the hymn’s sequence it follows hunger (क्षुधा, 5.26-28): the two basic drives of an embodied being.

Thirst in its wider sense, craving, is usually counted among the things that bind. The hymn does not exempt it. Medhas has already taught that Mahāmāyā herself draws even the minds of the wise into delusion (1.55–56) and is also the cause of release (1.57–58); in the Śākta reading the same Goddess rules what binds and what frees.

A modern reflection: to bow to the Goddess as thirst is not to praise craving. It is to see that even longing points beyond itself, and that the force which drives a creature toward what it lacks is not outside the divine.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as forbearance (क्षान्ति): the patience that bears injury without returning it.

Brahmā’s hymn in the first carita already calls her forbearance, in the same breath as modesty, contentment and peace (1.80: लज्जा पुष्टिस्तथा तुष्टिस्त्वं शान्तिः क्षान्तिरेव च). Several of those names return in this hymn as yā devī mantras (5.44, 5.47, 5.68).
A modern reflection: the gods praise forbearance while they are themselves dispossessed and waiting (5.2–7). Patience here is not passivity; it is the strength that holds out until help comes.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as जाति: birth, and the kind a being is born into. The word covers both the event (being born) and its result (belonging to a species, a lineage).

Two readings are current. One takes जाति as birth, the power by which beings come into existence; the other as the ‘kind’ that makes each creature what it is — in the philosophers’ language, the universal shared by all members of a class. Since the hymn speaks of ‘all beings’, the wider senses fit better than the later narrow sense of a social group.
A modern reflection: whatever one is born as, the hymn places the Goddess in that very fact of birth. No kind of being is outside her.

flags.uncertain: जाति can mean ‘birth’ or ‘kind, class’; the edition gives both and prefers neither strongly.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as modesty (लज्जा): the inner restraint that keeps a person from what is unworthy.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same word as a name: 740, लज्जा. The texts are separate; the shared name shows a shared Śākta idiom.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as peace (शान्ति): the stilling of agitation in every creature.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has शान्तिः as name 447, in a run of such qualities (443 तुष्टिः, 444 पुष्टिः, 445 मतिः, 446 धृतिः). Brahmā’s hymn here names her शान्तिः too (1.80).

comm.t: The Goddess is named as faith (श्रद्धा): the trust that sets the heart on what it holds true.

The gods said in chapter 4 that she is ‘faith in the good’ (4.5: श्रद्धा सतां). In the wider Hindu tradition faith shapes the person: the Bhagavad Gītā (17.3) says ‘a person is made of faith; as one’s faith is, so is one’ (श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः).
A modern reflection: on this reading faith is not only something a person has; it is a presence of the Goddess in the person. Trust itself becomes a place of meeting.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as Lakṣmī, fortune and prosperity, present in all beings. Prosperity is not a separate goddess’s gift here but one of her own forms.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as वृत्ति: the activity by which every being goes on living — its way of life, its means of sustenance.

Two senses are current. The common one is livelihood: what supports each creature’s life. Another takes वृत्ति as the movements of the mind (the Yoga term चित्तवृत्ति), so that every mental state is her form. The hymn’s neighbours (memory, faith, delusion) allow the second; the plain sense of ‘all beings’ favours the first.
A modern reflection: on either reading, ordinary work and ordinary thought are not outside the sacred. The means by which one lives is named as a form of the Goddess.

flags.uncertain: वृत्ति may be ‘livelihood, way of life’ or ‘a movement of the mind’; the edition prefers the first and notes the second.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as memory (स्मृति) in every creature.

Remembering her is the act this whole episode turns on: she had promised to destroy the gods’ calamities whenever they remembered her (5.6), and the gods’ hymn in chapter 4 says ‘remembered, you take away fear’ (4.17: दुर्गे स्मृता हरसि भीतिम्). Brahmā’s hymn calls her महास्मृतिः, the great memory (1.77). Here the power of remembering is itself her form.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has स्मृतिः as name 540.
A modern reflection: the faculty by which one turns to the divine is already the divine at work. Memory is not only a store of the past but a way back.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as compassion (दया), present in every creature that pities another.

The gods’ hymn in chapter 4 says she sends her weapons against enemies so that, purified by them, even they may reach the higher worlds (4.19), and concludes: ‘thus is compassion shown by you even to enemies’ (4.21: वैरिष्वपि प्रकटितैव दया त्वयेत्थम्). Compassion in the heart and ruthlessness in battle are found together in her alone (4.22).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has दयामूर्तिः ‘embodiment of compassion’ as name 581 — a compound rather than the bare word, but the same idea.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as the mother present in all beings: motherhood itself, in every creature that bears and nourishes young.

A modern reflection: the care of any mother for any child is named here as a form of the Goddess, not merely a picture of her.

mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as delusion: salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her — salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘As’ renders the instrumental -रूपेण ‘in the form of’; ‘delusion’ is chosen for भ्रान्ति (lit. ‘wandering, error’) because of the link with Mahāmāyā’s मोह in 1.55–56; ‘again and again’ renders नमो नमः.

comm.t: The last name of the yā devī series is error, delusion (भ्रान्ति): the confusion that takes one thing for another.

The series ends on its hardest case. Medhas taught that this Goddess, as Mahāmāyā, forcibly draws even the minds of the wise into delusion (1.55–56: ज्ञानिनामपि चेतांसि … बलादाकृष्य मोहाय महामाया प्रयच्छति) and is also the cause of release (1.57–58). To bow to her as delusion is to acknowledge that the power that confuses is hers, and so is the power to free.
A modern reflection: error is not praised; it is placed under the same sovereignty as knowledge. That is the ground for hoping that error can be undone.

samasa.literal: to the Goddess who is pervasion
samasa.sense: to the all-pervading Goddess — the name sums up the verse: she presides over the senses and is ever in all beings
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, व्याप्तेः देवी ‘the goddess of pervasion’. The karmadhāraya matches the pattern of the hymn, where each quality is her form.

samasa.sense: in all, without exception

morph.note: Agent noun in -तृ (तृच्) from अधि + √स्था ‘to stand over, preside’, made feminine with -ई (ङीप्): अधिष्ठातृ → अधिष्ठात्री. The s of the root turns to ṣ after the i of the prefix, and the following th becomes ṭh by ष्टुना ष्टुः (8.4.41): अधिष्ठा-. Like other agent nouns it takes the genitive of what is ruled (इन्द्रियाणाम्, भूतानाम्).
व्याप्ति is an action noun from वि + √आप् ‘to reach, pervade’ (svādi, 5P) with -ति (क्तिन्); i of वि becomes y before ā (इको यणचि, 6.1.77). देव्यै is the dative singular of the ī-stem देवी.

mantras.anvaya: या इन्द्रियाणाम् भूतानाम् च अधिष्ठात्री, अखिलेषु भूतेषु सततम् (व्याप्य स्थिता), तस्यै व्याप्तिदेव्यै नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … अधिष्ठात्री, … भूतेषु सततम्) with the correlative तस्यै व्याप्तिदेव्यै; the verb of being or pervading is understood and is supplied by the name व्याप्ति. भूत occurs twice: first (genitive, with इन्द्रियाणाम्) best as ‘the elements’, then (locative) as ‘beings’. Another construal takes भूतानाम् with इन्द्रियाणाम् — ‘ruler of the senses of beings’ — and च as joining the second clause.
mantras.lit: She who is the presiding power of the senses and of the elements, and who is always in all beings — to her, the Goddess who is pervasion, homage, homage.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who rules the senses and the elements, and who ever pervades all beings — to her, the all-pervading Goddess, salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Pervades’ is supplied from the name व्याप्तिदेवी; the Sanskrit has no verb in the second clause.

comm.t: After the twenty-one yā devī mantras, a full two-line śloka sums them up: the Goddess presides over the senses and the elements and is constantly present in every being. Her name here is व्याप्तिदेवी, the pervading Goddess.

In the Gita Press count this is a single mantra (a śloka), not a three-part one, though it ends with the same नमो नमः. The pairing of senses (इन्द्रिय) and elements (भूत) recalls the Sāṃkhya list of principles from which body and world are made; the verse places a single presiding power over both.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has व्यापिनी ‘the pervading one’ as name 400 — the same idea in a different form of the word.

flags.uncertain: भूतानाम् may be ‘of the elements’ (coordinated with इन्द्रियाणाम्) or ‘of beings’ (‘the senses of beings’); the edition prefers the first because of च.

samasa.literal: by the form that is consciousness
samasa.sense: as consciousness itself
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, चितेः रूपम् ‘the form of consciousness’; the karmadhāraya fits the hymn’s pattern.

morph.note: Absolutive of वि + √आप्: with a prefix the absolutive takes -य (ल्यप्) instead of -त्वा. The i of वि becomes y before ā (व्याप्य). ‘Having pervaded’ — here simply ‘pervading’, since the pervading and the abiding are not successive.
Past passive participle of √स्था (ā → i before -त), as संस्थिता in the yā devī mantras but without the prefix: ‘(who) stands, abides’, with अस्ति understood.
चिति is an action noun from √चित् ‘to perceive, be aware’ (bhvādi, 1P, चेतति) with -ति (क्तिन्): consciousness, awareness.

mantras.anvaya: या चितिरूपेण एतत् कृत्स्नम् जगत् व्याप्य स्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The yā devī form returns, but the relative clause is new: या … व्याप्य स्थिता, with जगत् as the object of the absolutive. The second line is the familiar three mantras (78, 79, 80).
mantras.lit: She who, in the form of consciousness, abides pervading this entire world — homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.
mantras.tr: To her who, as consciousness, pervades this whole world and abides in it: salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her — salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: The absolutive व्याप्य ‘having pervaded’ is rendered as a present (‘pervades’), since the pervading and the abiding are simultaneous.

comm.t: The last three-part mantra widens the view from ‘all beings’ to ‘this whole world’ and names her most basic form: consciousness (चिति), pervading everything.

With this mantra the three-part mantras of the chapter reach twenty-two — twenty-one yā devī mantras and this one — which the colophon counts as sixty-six mantras. The gods’ hymn in chapter 4 opened on the same thought: ‘the Goddess by whose own power this world is spread out’ (4.3: देव्या यया ततमिदं जगदात्मशक्त्या).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has चितिः as name 362. The idea that the Goddess is consciousness itself is shared across Śākta texts; the two works remain distinct.
A modern reflection: after naming her in hunger, thirst, faith and error, the hymn names what all of them have in common — awareness. Every state named before is a state of consciousness.

samasa.sense: because they had gained their desire through her (in the Mahiṣa episode), or: for the refuge they wanted
samasa.alt: संश्रय can mean ‘attaining, coming to’ or ‘refuge, resort’. Taken as ‘refuge’ the phrase means ‘(praised) for the sake of the refuge they desired’ (अभीष्टः संश्रयः, a karmadhāraya). The ablative of cause with ‘attainment of the desired’ fits पूर्वम्: the gods praised her once their wish had been granted.

mantras.anvaya: पूर्वम् अभीष्टसंश्रयात् सुरैः स्तुता, तथा सुरेन्द्रेण दिनेषु सेविता, शुभहेतुः सा ईश्वरी नः शुभानि भद्राणि करोतु, आपदः च अभिहन्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two participial phrases (स्तुता … सेविता) describe the subject सा ईश्वरी; the main verbs are two imperatives of prayer, करोतु and अभिहन्तु, joined by च. The sentence runs on into 5.82, whose relative clauses (या …) also describe सा.
mantras.lit: Praised formerly by the gods because of the attainment of their desire, and likewise served by the lord of the gods for days — may she, the Sovereign, the cause of good, do auspicious things and blessings for us, and strike down calamities.
mantras.tr: She whom the gods once praised when their desire was granted, and whom Indra, lord of the gods, worshipped day after day — may that Sovereign, the source of all good, bring us what is auspicious and blessed, and strike down our calamities.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Our’ with calamities is supplied from नः; the Sanskrit has नः once, with करोतु.

comm.t: The gods close their hymn with a prayer. They recall that they praised her before — after the slaying of Mahiṣa, when their desire was granted (chapter 4) — and that Indra worshipped her for days; now they ask her to bring them good and strike down their calamities. The metre changes for this closing prayer: vaṃśastha (twelve syllables to the line, ja-ta-ja-ra) after the anuṣṭubh of the hymn.

The prayer echoes the chapter 4 hymn, led by Śakra (Indra, 4.2), where the gods asked ‘may she bestow auspicious things on us’ (4.3: विदधातु शुभानि सा नः). Her promise in 5.6 — to destroy the gods’ calamities whenever they remembered her — is what they now invoke.

mantras.anvaya: (सा ईश्वरी नः शुभानि करोतु) या साम्प्रतम् च उद्धतदैत्यतापितैः अस्माभिः सुरैः ईशा च नमस्यते, या च भक्तिविनम्रमूर्तिभिः स्मृता तत्क्षणम् एव नः सर्वापदः हन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two relative clauses (या … नमस्यते; या च … हन्ति) still describe सा ईश्वरी of 5.81, whose prayer (करोतु, अभिहन्तु) governs the whole. The first च sets ‘now’ against ‘formerly’ in 5.81; the second च goes with ईशा (‘and, as Sovereign, is bowed to’); the third joins the second clause.
mantras.lit: She who now, too, is bowed to as Sovereign by us, the gods, tormented by the arrogant daityas; and who, remembered by those whose bodies are bowed in devotion, at that very moment destroys all our calamities —
mantras.tr: She to whom we gods, harried by the arrogant daityas, now bow as Sovereign, and who, the moment she is remembered by those bowed down in devotion, destroys all our calamities — (may she bring us good).
mantras.tr_note: The bracketed close is supplied from 5.81 (करोतु … अभिहन्तु); 5.82 has no main verb of its own.

comm.t: The hymn ends with two relative clauses on the Goddess of 5.81: she is bowed to now by the gods tormented by the daityas, and she destroys every calamity the instant she is remembered in devotion. The prayer of 5.81 governs both. The metre is indravaṃśā (ta-ta-ja-ra), the sister of the vaṃśastha of 5.81, differing only in the first syllable of each line.

The verse restates her promise of 5.6 — ‘remembered in calamities, I will destroy your greatest calamities at that very moment’ (तत्क्षणात्) — as a fact about her: स्मृता तत्क्षणमेव हन्ति. The hymn is answered at once: when the narrative resumes (5.84), Pārvatī comes to bathe in the Gaṅgā where the gods are praising.
A modern reflection: the hymn moves from praise to petition only at its end. The gods first name her in everything — hunger, faith, error, consciousness — and only then ask for help.

flags.uncertain: ईशा is taken as a feminine title (‘the Sovereign’); an instrumental of ईश् ‘lord’ (Indra) is grammatically possible. The second च is then loosely placed.

morph.note: Perfect of √या (ययौ, with the -au ending of ā-roots) behind two prefixes: अभि + आ, where i becomes y before ā (अभ्या-). ‘Came up to, approached’.
Infinitive in -tum of √स्ना, expressing purpose with a verb of motion: ‘came to bathe’.
With the participle-like adjective स्तवादियुक्तानाम् it forms a genitive absolute: ‘the gods being so engaged’, i.e. ‘while the gods were praising’.

mantras.anvaya: नृपनन्दन, एवं देवानां स्तवादियुक्तानां (सताम्) तत्र पार्वती जाह्नव्याः तोये स्नातुम् अभ्याययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: A genitive absolute (एवं … देवानाम्) sets the time; the main clause is पार्वती … अभ्याययौ with the purpose infinitive स्नातुम्; नृपनन्दन is the narrator’s address.
mantras.lit: While the gods were thus engaged in praise and the rest, there Pārvatī came, O son of a king, to bathe in the water of the Jāhnavī.
mantras.tr: While the gods were thus praising, O prince, Pārvatī came there to bathe in the waters of the Gaṅgā.

comm.t: The scene shifts while the hymn is still in the air: Pārvatī, Śiva’s consort and the daughter of Himavat, comes down to the Gaṅgā to bathe at the very place where the gods are praying. The genitive absolute ties the two events together.

Chapter 4 announced this episode in advance: the Goddess would arise again ‘from the body of Gaurī’ to kill Śumbha and Niśumbha (4.41, गौरीदेहात्). Pārvatī’s coming to the river is the occasion for that promise to be kept.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name, पार्वती (name 246). The two works share the Śākta identification of the Goddess with Himavat’s daughter; they remain distinct texts.

morph.note: Imperfect of √ब्रू with augment a- and the connecting ī that ब्रू takes before consonant endings of the strong forms: अ-ब्रव्-ई-त्. The verse uses it twice, once for each speaker.

The suffix -tas (tasil) makes an indeclinable with ablative sense: ‘from the body’s sheath’. It still governs a genitive (अस्याः), as a noun would.

mantras.anvaya: सुभ्रूः सा तान् सुरान् अब्रवीत् — अत्र भवद्भिः का स्तूयते (इति)। अस्याः शरीरकोशतः समुद्भूता शिवा च अब्रवीत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences of the same shape: subject, अब्रवीत्. The first carries Pārvatī’s question as direct speech; the second introduces the answer, which is given in 5.86.
mantras.lit: She, the fair-browed one, said to those gods: ‘Who is being praised by you here?’ And Śivā, having come forth from the sheath of her body, said:
mantras.tr: The lovely-browed Goddess asked the gods, ‘Whom are you praising here?’ And from the sheath of her own body Śivā came forth and answered:

comm.t: Pārvatī asks whom the gods are praising, and the answer comes not from them but from a goddess who steps out of Pārvatī’s own body. The one who asks and the one who answers are of one substance; the reply follows in 5.86.
Traditionally the question is read as the Goddess’s play (līlā): she asks as though she did not know, so that she herself may reveal that the gods’ hymn was addressed to her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names the Goddess सुभ्रूः (name 461) and शिवा (name 53). The shared epithets belong to a common Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate.

mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: subject स्तोत्रम्, verb क्रियते, agent देवैः with three qualifiers (निराकृतैः, समेतैः, पराजितैः).
mantras.lit: This hymn to me is being made by the gods, assembled, driven out by the daitya Śumbha and defeated in battle by Niśumbha.
mantras.tr: ‘This hymn is offered to me by the gods, who have gathered here after the demon Śumbha drove them out and Niśumbha defeated them in battle.’
mantras.tr_note: ‘After’ makes explicit the order of events implied by the three participles.

comm.t: Śivā answers Pārvatī’s question: the hymn is hers. The gods are named by their plight — expelled by Śumbha, beaten in battle by Niśumbha — which recalls the opening of the chapter (5.2–5).

The tradition reads the episode as a statement of identity: the Goddess the gods invoked as dwelling in all beings (5.14–80) answers from within Pārvatī herself. Asking and answering, she shows that the hymn and its object are hers.

mantras.anvaya: यत् तस्याः पार्वत्याः शरीरकोशात् अम्बिका निःसृता, ततः (सा) समस्तेषु लोकेषु कौशिकी इति गीयते।
mantras.anvaya_en: A causal pair: यत् … निःसृता (‘since she came forth …’) and ततः … गीयते (‘therefore she is sung of …’).
mantras.lit: Since Ambikā came forth from the sheath of the body of that Pārvatī, she is therefore sung of in all the worlds as ‘Kauśikī’.
mantras.tr: Because Ambikā emerged from the sheath of Pārvatī’s body, she is celebrated in all the worlds as Kauśikī.

comm.t: Medhas explains the name: the goddess who emerged (Śivā of 5.85, now called Ambikā) is Kauśikī because she came out of Pārvatī’s bodily sheath (kośa). From here the text mostly calls her Ambikā or Devī.

In the Gita Press pāṭha, the dhyāna printed before chapter 5 describes the presiding Goddess of the third carita, Mahāsarasvatī, as गौरीदेहसमुद्भवाम् ‘born from the body of Gaurī’ — this very emergence. The assignment of Mahāsarasvatī to the carita is liturgical tradition.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also calls the Goddess अम्बिका (name 295). The Devī Māhātmya’s own story of Kauśikī belongs to this text; the shared name does not import the other hymn’s theology.

morph.note: Locative absolute (with तस्याम्): ‘she having gone out’, i.e. ‘when she had emerged’. The participle of वि + निर् + √गम् loses the root’s m before -ta (गत).
Root aorist of √भू with a predicate adjective: कृष्णा अभूत् ‘became dark’.

mantras.anvaya: तस्यां तु विनिर्गतायां सा पार्वती अपि कृष्णा अभूत्, (सा) कालिका इति समाख्याता हिमाचलकृताश्रया (च अभूत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (तस्यां विनिर्गतायाम्) gives the moment; the main clause is सा पार्वती … कृष्णा अभूत्, with two further qualifiers of Pārvatī in the second line.
mantras.lit: And when she had gone out, that Pārvatī too became dark; called ‘Kālikā’, she made her dwelling on the Himālaya.
mantras.tr: When Ambikā had come forth, Pārvatī herself turned dark. Known as Kālikā, she took up her abode on the Himālaya.

comm.t: Once the radiant Ambikā has left her, Pārvatī becomes dark and is called Kālikā; she remains on the Himālaya. The narrative now follows Ambikā; Kālikā does not act again in this chapter.

Kālikā here is Pārvatī after the emergence, not the Kālī who later springs from Ambikā’s brow to fight Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (7.5–6). Other Purāṇic tellings reverse the colours — the dark sheath becomes Kauśikī and Pārvatī becomes fair Gaurī — but this text says plainly that Ambikā came out and Pārvatī became dark.

mantras.anvaya_en: Verb ददर्श, its object अम्बिकाम् with the participle phrase परं रूपं बिभ्राणाम् सुमनोहरम्, and the double subject चण्डः मुण्डः च with the apposition भृत्यौ.
mantras.lit: Then Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the two servants of Śumbha and Niśumbha, saw Ambikā bearing a supreme, most captivating form.
mantras.tr: Then Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, servants of Śumbha and Niśumbha, saw Ambikā in her surpassing, enchanting beauty.

comm.t: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa enter the story as servants of the demon brothers. Their seeing of the Goddess sets the whole uttama carita in motion: report, embassy and war.

The same two servants lead the first army against her (7.2) and die by Kālī; Caṇḍikā then names Kālī ‘Cāmuṇḍā’ after them (7.27). The pair who first look on her beauty become the occasion of one of her best-known names.

mantras.lit: And she was reported by those two to Śumbha: ‘Some exceedingly captivating woman, O great king, is staying (there), illuminating the Himālaya.’
mantras.tr: They told Śumbha of her: ‘Great king, there is a woman of surpassing beauty dwelling on the Himālaya, lighting up the mountain.’

comm.t: The servants’ report to Śumbha begins; it runs to 5.100. They know nothing of who she is — she is ‘some woman’ (का अपि स्त्री) — only that her radiance lights up the mountain.
A modern reading: the demons see the Goddess only as a beautiful woman, and the whole embassy that follows rests on that misreading — the divine taken for an object to be acquired.

mantras.lit: Such supreme beauty has never been seen by anyone anywhere. Let it be found out who this goddess is, and let her be seized, O lord of the asuras.
mantras.tr: ‘Never has anyone, anywhere, seen beauty so perfect. Find out who this goddess may be, lord of the asuras, and take her.’

comm.t: The servants press their case: her beauty is beyond anything ever seen, so Śumbha should discover who she is and take her. They call her देवी, ‘goddess’, without understanding the word.
A modern reading: the servants move in one breath from wonder to seizure — ‘find out who she is, and take her’. The story will show how little that grasping understands.

mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause सा तु तिष्ठति with three descriptions of her in the first line; a second clause भवान् … अर्हति with its infinitive.
mantras.lit: A jewel among women, exceedingly lovely of limb, lighting up the quarters with her radiance — she is there, O lord of the daityas; your honour ought to see her.
mantras.tr: ‘A jewel among women, perfect in every limb, she lights the whole horizon with her splendour. There she stays, lord of the demons — you should see her.’

comm.t: The servants describe her a second time and urge Śumbha to go and look. The phrase स्त्रीरत्नम् ‘jewel among women’ prepares the argument that follows: Śumbha owns every jewel of the three worlds (5.93–99), so this one too should be his.

The word ratna governs the whole report and the messenger’s speech that follows (5.109–113): Śumbha is a ‘consumer of jewels’ (रत्नभुजः, 5.112). The Goddess’s light, which the hymn praised, is seen by the demons only as a treasure.

mantras.lit: Whatever jewels, gems, elephants, horses and the like there are in the three worlds, O lord, all of them now shine in your house.
mantras.tr: ‘Lord, every treasure of the three worlds — jewels, gems, elephants, horses and all the rest — now shines in your palace.’

comm.t: The servants begin the catalogue of Śumbha’s plunder (5.93–99). The general statement comes first: every treasure of the three worlds is now in his house.

The list fills out what the chapter’s opening stated briefly: the brothers took over the offices of Indra, the Sun, the Moon, Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, Vāyu and Agni (5.2–4). Each treasure named below belonged to one of those gods.

mantras.lit: Airāvata, the jewel among elephants, has been brought from Purandara; and this Pārijāta tree, and likewise the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
mantras.tr: ‘Airāvata, finest of elephants, has been taken from Indra; so too this Pārijāta tree, and the horse Uccaiḥśravas.’

comm.t: The first spoils named are Indra’s: his elephant Airāvata, the Pārijāta tree of his heaven, and the horse Uccaiḥśravas.

All three are treasures that came up from the churning of the ocean; the messenger himself says so of the horse (5.110, क्षीरोदमथनोद्भूतम्). Possessing them, Śumbha has taken the visible marks of Indra’s kingship.

mantras.lit: This swan-yoked aerial car, a very jewel, brought here, stands in your courtyard — that which was the wonder of Vedhas.
mantras.tr: ‘In your courtyard stands this swan-drawn chariot of the skies, a true treasure brought here — once the marvel of Brahmā.’

comm.t: Next is Brahmā’s own vehicle: the aerial car drawn by swans, now parked in Śumbha’s courtyard. Even the Creator has been stripped.
The swan (haṃsa) is Brahmā’s mount in Purāṇic iconography; its car here shows that the demons’ conquest reached beyond Indra’s heaven to the Creator himself.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: a participial one (निधिः … समानीतः) and a finite one with ददौ, whose object मालाम् has two qualifiers.
mantras.lit: This treasure, Mahāpadma, has been brought from the lord of wealth; and the Ocean gave a garland full of filaments, of unfading lotuses.
mantras.tr: ‘This treasure, the Mahāpadma, was taken from Kubera; and the Ocean gave you a garland of never-fading lotuses, fresh with their filaments.’
mantras.tr_note: ‘You’ is supplied: the Ocean’s gift is to Śumbha, as the context makes clear.

comm.t: Kubera, lord of wealth, has lost the Mahāpadma, and the Ocean has given a garland of unfading lotuses. The Ocean’s gift is phrased as a gift (ददौ), not a seizure: the conquered gods now pay tribute.
Classical lists of Kubera’s nine treasures (nidhi) include Mahāpadma. Its loss marks the seizure of Kubera’s office, one of those named at the chapter’s opening (कौबेरम्, 5.3).

mantras.lit: Varuṇa’s parasol, streaming gold, stands in your house; likewise this finest of chariots, which formerly was Prajāpati’s.
mantras.tr: ‘Varuṇa’s parasol, raining gold, stands in your palace, and so does this superb chariot that once belonged to Prajāpati.’

comm.t: Varuṇa’s gold-showering parasol and Prajāpati’s chariot complete the list of royal insignia. The parasol is the classic sign of sovereignty; its owner has lost his rule (वरुणस्य, 5.3).

mantras.lit: The spear of Death named Utkrāntidā has been taken by you, O lord; the noose of the king of the waters is in your brother’s possession.

comm.t: Now the weapons: Yama’s spear Utkrāntidā, ‘giver of the soul’s departure’, taken by Śumbha, and Varuṇa’s noose, held by Niśumbha. Śumbha and his brother between them hold the instruments of death and of binding.
Both seizures fill out the opening statement of the chapter, that the brothers took the offices of Yama (याम्यम्) and Varuṇa (वरुणस्य) (5.3).

mantras.lit: Having heard these words of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, Śumbha then sent the great asura Sugrīva as messenger to the Devī.
mantras.tr: Hearing what Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa said, Śumbha sent the mighty demon Sugrīva as his envoy to the Goddess.

comm.t: Śumbha acts at once on the report: he does not go to see her, as the servants urged (5.92), but sends an envoy, the asura Sugrīva. His instructions follow in 5.103.

The embassy gives the chapter its name in the colophon, देव्या दूतसंवादः ‘the Goddess’s dialogue with the messenger’. Sugrīva the demon is a different figure from the monkey-king of the Rāmāyaṇa who bears the same name.

mantras.tr: ‘Go to her and tell her this and this from me; and act quickly, so that she comes to me willingly.’
mantras.tr_note: The gerundives are rendered as imperatives addressed to the messenger, which is their force.

comm.t: Śumbha’s instructions to Sugrīva, given without a speaker label: speak to her on my authority, and bring her quickly and willingly. इति च इति च stands for the message itself, which the envoy delivers in full in 5.106–114.
A modern reading: Śumbha wants her consent (सम्प्रीत्या, ‘gladly’) but only as a means — ‘arrange it so that she comes’. Courtesy put to the service of possession is still possession.

mantras.tr: ‘Goddess, Śumbha, lord of the demons, is supreme sovereign of the three worlds. I am his envoy, sent by him, and have come here before you.’

comm.t: Sugrīva opens with protocol: he names his master’s title and his own office. Śumbha is called परमेश्वरः, ‘supreme lord’, in the three worlds.

A modern reading: the title is ironic in context. The gods’ hymn has just praised the Goddess as the power within all beings, and the one the envoy addresses as ‘Devī’ is the sovereign he does not recognise.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess परमेश्वरी (name 396), the feminine of the title Śumbha claims here. The comparison is ours; the Devī Māhātmya itself makes the irony through its story.

mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यः … अव्याहताज्ञः) and a second epithet describe the subject सः; inside the main clause a second relative pair (यत् … तत्) makes the object of the imperative शृणुष्व.
mantras.lit: He who always (has) unobstructed command among all the divine orders, (and) who has conquered all the enemies of the Daityas — hear that which he says.
mantras.tr: Among all the orders of heavenly beings his command is never resisted, and he has vanquished every foe of the Daityas. Hear what he says.
mantras.tr_note: The relative clause is turned into two plain statements.

comm.t: The messenger Sugrīva, sent by Śumbha (5.102–104), finishes introducing his master (5.106) before delivering the message. The two titles summarise the opening of the chapter: the brothers have taken the gods’ offices and driven them out (5.2–5).

देवयोनि is the usual name for the superhuman orders below the gods proper; the lexicon Amarakośa lists ten (vidyādharas, apsarases, yakṣas, rakṣases, gandharvas, kinnaras, piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas and bhūtas). The claim is that every such order obeys Śumbha.
A modern reading: the message is preceded by credentials. Power announces itself before it asks, so that the asking sounds like a favour.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses, the first two nominal (the verb ‘is / are’ understood), the third with the finite verb उपाश्नामि. From here to 5.114 the messenger speaks in Śumbha’s first person.
mantras.lit: Mine is the entire triple world; mine are the gods, following my will. All the shares of the sacrifice I enjoy, each separately.
mantras.tr: “The three worlds are mine entire, and the gods obey my will. Every share of the sacrifice, one by one, is mine to enjoy.
mantras.tr_note: The opening quotation mark shows that the message is quoted in Śumbha’s own words.

comm.t: The message proper begins, in Śumbha’s voice. Its claims repeat the narrator’s account at the head of the chapter: the three worlds and the sacrificial shares were taken from Indra (5.2), and the gods were driven out (5.4–5).

The sacrificial share (यज्ञभाग) is the gods’ sustenance and the sign of their office. In the Purāṇic view, a demon who eats the shares has overturned the order of the world, not merely won a war; the Devī’s own message in 8.26 demands that the gods again be ‘eaters of oblations’ (हविर्भुजः), and 12.34 records that they enjoyed their shares once more.

mantras.anvaya: त्रैलोक्ये (यानि) वररत्नानि (तानि) अशेषतः मम वश्यानि (सन्ति); तथा एव देवेन्द्रवाहनं गजरत्नं च (मया) हृत्वा (मम वश्यम्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a nominal sentence (verb understood). The second hangs on the absolutive हृत्वा and borrows its predicate from the first: the elephant too is ‘subject to me’.
mantras.lit: In the three worlds the choice jewels are subject to me without exception; and likewise the jewel of elephants, the mount of the lord of the gods, having seized (it) —
mantras.tr: Every treasure of worth in the three worlds belongs to me, without exception — so too the king of elephants, Indra’s own mount, which I have taken.
mantras.tr_note: The absolutive हृत्वा is rendered as a relative clause ‘which I have taken’, completing the loose syntax.

comm.t: Śumbha’s message repeats what Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa told him (5.93–94): the jewels of the three worlds are in his palace, and Indra’s elephant Airāvata among them. The messenger turns their report into a boast.

रत्न ‘jewel’ in this passage means the best of any kind — elephant, horse, tree, woman — not only gems. The list prepares the inference of 5.112: if all jewels are his, the ‘jewel of women’ must be his too.

Absolutive with prefixes, so -य (lyap). In a passive sentence its subject is the agent in the instrumental: the gods bowed, then handed over the horse.

The horse’s name is the s-stem उच्चैःश्रवस्; in this compound it appears as उच्चैःश्रवस-, as if an a-stem, a by-form found in epic and Purāṇic usage. The visarga of उच्चैः is kept inside the compound, as printed.

mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: subject अश्वरत्नम् with three qualifiers, agent अमरैः, recipient मम, predicate समर्पितम्; the absolutive प्रणिपत्य belongs to the agent.
mantras.lit: That jewel of horses called Uccaiḥśravas, which arose from the churning of the Milk Ocean, was handed over to me by the immortals, having bowed down.
mantras.tr: Uccaiḥśravas, the finest of horses, born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, the gods themselves surrendered to me with bowed heads.

comm.t: The second of Indra’s great treasures: the horse Uccaiḥśravas, already listed by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (5.94). Śumbha adds a detail they did not give — the gods bowed as they handed it over.

Uccaiḥśravas is one of the treasures that rose from the ocean when the gods and asuras churned it, and belongs to Indra in the Purāṇic accounts. A treasure won by the gods from that churning is now given up to an asura: the boast measures how complete his victory is.

mantras.lit: And whatever other things that are jewels (there are) among the gods, the Gandharvas and the serpents — they (are) in me alone, O beautiful one.
mantras.tr: And whatever else ranks as a jewel among gods, Gandharvas and serpents — all of it, lovely one, rests with me alone.

comm.t: The list of treasures closes with a general claim: every ‘jewel’ of every race is now in Śumbha’s possession. The vocative शोभने turns the boast towards the Devī.
The Devī is addressed first as ‘beautiful’; in the next verse she is placed among the jewels. The argument is the one Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa made (5.100): all jewels are his, so why not this one?

mantras.anvaya: देवि, वयं लोके त्वां स्त्रीरत्नभूतां मन्यामहे। यतः वयं रत्नभुजः, (अतः) सा त्वम् अस्मान् उपागच्छ।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence has a double accusative (त्वाम् … स्त्रीरत्नभूताम्). The second is an imperative with a causal clause (यतः …) giving the reason.
mantras.lit: We regard you, O Devī, as being the jewel among women in the world. Such as you are, come to us, since we are the enjoyers of jewels.
mantras.tr: We hold you, O Devī, to be the jewel among the women of the world. Come to us, then, for jewels are ours to enjoy.

comm.t: The argument of the message is now explicit: every jewel belongs to Śumbha, the Devī is the jewel among women, therefore she must come to him. Śumbha speaks of himself in the plural (वयम्), as a king.

The word रत्न has carried the whole speech from 5.109. The tradition reads the irony of the scene: the one he names a ‘jewel’ to be owned is the power by whom, in the narrator’s words of 5.116, the world itself is upheld.

mantras.lit: Choose me, or else my younger brother Niśumbha of wide valour, O you of darting glances — since you are indeed a jewel.
mantras.tr: Take me, or my younger brother Niśumbha of mighty valour, O lady of the darting glance — for a jewel is what you are.

comm.t: The proposal itself: the Devī may choose either brother. The reason is the same as in 5.112 — she is a jewel, and jewels go to the brothers.

The offer of a choice between two husbands prepares the Devī’s answer: she will lay down one condition for either of them (5.120–121). The narrative leaves both brothers in the frame; both will meet her, but only in battle (chapters 9–10).

The abstract suffix -ता (tal) makes a feminine noun of state from the compound: ‘my-consort-ness’. With a verb of motion (व्रज) the accusative names the condition one passes into: ‘go to the state of …’, i.e. ‘become …’.

mantras.anvaya: मत्परिग्रहात् (त्वम्) अतुलं परमैश्वर्यं प्राप्स्यसे। एतत् बुद्ध्या समालोच्य मत्परिग्रहतां व्रज।
mantras.anvaya_en: A promise in the future (प्राप्स्यसे), then an imperative (व्रज) preceded by an absolutive (समालोच्य) with its object एतत्.
mantras.lit: You will obtain supreme, matchless sovereignty from being taken by me. Having considered this well with your understanding, go to the state of being my consort.
mantras.tr: As my wife you will gain a sovereignty beyond compare. Weigh this well in your mind, and become my consort.”
mantras.tr_note: The closing quotation mark ends the message quoted in Śumbha’s words (from 5.108).

comm.t: The message ends with an inducement and a command: marriage to Śumbha will give the Devī matchless power; she should think it over and consent.

The offer reverses the truth the text has already stated: the gods’ hymn has just praised her as the power present in all beings (5.14–80), and the narrator will call her the one by whom the world is upheld (5.116). Śumbha offers her what is already hers.
A modern reading: the appeal to ‘consider it with your intelligence’ invites calculation. The Devī will answer not with a calculation but with a vow made long before (5.119–120).

mantras.lit: Thus addressed, the Devī then, grave and smiling within, spoke — Durgā, the Blessed, the Auspicious, by whom this world is upheld.
mantras.tr: So addressed, the Devī — Durgā, the Blessed, the Auspicious, by whom this world is upheld — grave of face yet smiling inwardly, gave her answer.
mantras.tr_note: The appositive names are brought forward next to देवी.

comm.t: The narrator introduces the Devī’s reply. The contrast is marked: she is grave, but smiles within. The second line steps out of the scene to remind the hearer who is being asked to marry Śumbha — the one by whom the world is upheld.

The hidden smile is read as the key to her reply: what she says will be courteous and literally true, while its meaning is the opposite of surrender. The name Durgā, ‘hard to approach’, is apt at the very moment an asura proposes to take her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has two of the names given here: 190, दुर्गा, and 279, भगवती. The coincidence of names reflects a shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two passive statements with the participles उक्तम् and उदितम् (verb ‘is’ understood), then two nominal sentences.
mantras.lit: Truth has been spoken by you; nothing false at all has been uttered by you here. Śumbha is the overlord of the three worlds, and Niśumbha too is such.
mantras.tr: What you say is true; you have spoken no falsehood here. Śumbha is lord of the three worlds, and Niśumbha is his equal.

comm.t: The Devī begins by granting everything the messenger has said about the brothers’ power. She does not dispute their rank; her objection will lie elsewhere.

Read with the smile of 5.116, the concession is ironic: she accepts the facts in order to bring in a condition the facts cannot meet. Note that 5.128, as the Gita Press prints it, does not repeat the phrase निशुम्भश्चापि तादृशः, though other witnesses read it there too (see 5.128).

mantras.lit: But here — what has been vowed, how is that to be made false? Let the vow be heard which was made formerly out of little understanding.
mantras.tr: But in this matter there is a vow I made, and how could I break it? Hear the promise I once made, foolishly.
mantras.tr_note: The passive constructions are turned active (‘I made’, ‘could I break’); the agent ‘I’ is implied by the context.

comm.t: The Devī introduces an obstacle: a vow she made long ago. She cannot make it false, and she calls it the product of her ‘little understanding’.

The self-deprecation is read as irony matching her inward smile (5.116): the Goddess who is praised as बुद्धि itself (5.20) claims to have acted from small understanding. The vow is not a mistake but the trap into which the asuras will walk.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three relative clauses, each opened by यः, all taken up by the single correlative सः of the main clause.
mantras.lit: He who conquers me in battle, he who removes my pride, he who is my match in strength in the world — he will be my husband.
mantras.tr: “He who conquers me in battle, who humbles my pride, who is my equal in strength in all the world — he shall be my husband.”
mantras.tr_note: Set in quotation marks as the words of the vow announced in 5.119.

comm.t: The vow itself, in three conditions that come to one: the husband must defeat her in battle, break her pride, and match her strength. The repetition of यः … यः … यः gives it the form of a formal pledge.

Since the text has already shown her to be the power of all the gods together (2.9–30) and the power present in all beings (5.14–80), no one can meet the condition. The tradition reads the vow as a statement of her sovereignty: the Goddess is not won as a possession, and her only ‘husband’ would be her equal.
A modern reading: the Devī answers a claim of ownership with a test of strength. She does not argue with Śumbha’s logic of jewels; she changes the terms on which it can be applied.

The urgency (किं चिरेण, लघु) mirrors the messenger’s demand that she come quickly (5.103, लघु). The invitation is a challenge: the next chapters bring first the asura generals and finally the two brothers to fight her.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, त्वम् अवलिप्ता असि; मम अग्रतः एवं मा ब्रूहि। त्रैलोक्ये कः पुमान् शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः अग्रे तिष्ठेत्?
mantras.anvaya_en: A statement, a prohibition (मा … ब्रूहि), and a rhetorical question with the optative.
mantras.lit: You are arrogant, O Devī; do not speak thus in front of me. In the three worlds what man could stand before Śumbha and Niśumbha?
mantras.tr: You are proud, O Devī. Do not speak so in my presence. What man in the three worlds could stand before Śumbha and Niśumbha?

comm.t: The messenger takes the vow as arrogance (अवलिप्ता) and rejects it: no man in the three worlds can face the two brothers, so a contest is absurd.

The word दर्प ‘pride’ of the vow (5.120) is answered with अवलिप्ता ‘puffed up’. The irony runs the other way in the narrative: it is the asuras’ pride that will be removed, in the battles of chapters 6–10. Śumbha himself will make the same charge at the end, बलावलेपात् ‘from pride in strength’ (10.3).

mantras.anvaya: देवि, सर्वे देवाः अन्येषाम् अपि दैत्यानां सम्मुखे युधि न वै तिष्ठन्ति; एकिका स्त्री त्वं किं पुनः?
mantras.anvaya_en: A negative statement followed by the elliptical rhetorical question किं पुनः (‘how much less [will] you …’), whose verb is understood from तिष्ठन्ति.
mantras.lit: All the gods do not indeed stand in battle face to face even with other Daityas, O Devī — how much less you, a woman, alone?
mantras.tr: Not all the gods together can stand in battle even before the lesser Daityas, O Devī — how much less you, a woman, alone!
mantras.tr_note: अन्येषाम् ‘other’ is rendered ‘lesser’ to bring out the contrast with Śumbha and Niśumbha.

comm.t: The messenger argues from the greater to the lesser: the gods cannot face even the other Daityas; a lone woman cannot face the brothers.

Being alone and a woman is, for the messenger, the decisive weakness. The narrative will turn both against the asuras: Śumbha will taunt her for relying on other goddesses, and she will withdraw them all into herself to fight alone (10.3–6).

mantras.anvaya: येषां (सम्मुखे) संयुगे इन्द्राद्याः सकलाः देवाः न तस्थुः, तेषां शुम्भादीनां सम्मुखं (त्वं) स्त्री कथं प्रयास्यसि?
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (येषां … न तस्थुः) names the asuras; the main clause is a rhetorical question with the future प्रयास्यसि, its subject ‘you’ implied.
mantras.lit: Of whom in battle all the gods headed by Indra did not stand (before) — how will you, a woman, go to the front of those, Śumbha and the rest?
mantras.tr: Indra and all the gods could not hold their ground in battle against Śumbha and his host. How will you, a woman, go out to face them?
mantras.tr_note: The relative construction is turned into two sentences.

comm.t: The messenger repeats his argument with a fact the hearer knows: Indra and all the gods were defeated by these asuras (5.2–5). How then can a woman go out against them?

The listener has just heard the same defeated gods praise the Devī as the power behind all beings (5.9–82). The messenger’s reasoning measures her against the gods; the text has already placed her above them.

mantras.anvaya: सा त्वं मया एव उक्ता (सती) शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः पार्श्वं गच्छ; केशाकर्षणनिर्धूतगौरवा (सती) मा गमिष्यसि।
mantras.anvaya_en: An imperative (गच्छ) and a prohibitive future (मा गमिष्यसि) set against each other: go now willingly, not later by force.
mantras.lit: So go, bidden by me alone, to the side of Śumbha and Niśumbha; do not go (later) with your dignity shaken off by the dragging of your hair.
mantras.tr: Go, then, to Śumbha and Niśumbha now, at my word alone — lest you go dragged there by the hair, stripped of your honour.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Now’ and ‘later’ (lit.) and ‘lest’ (tr) bring out the contrast of the two verbs; they are implied, not stated.

comm.t: The messenger ends with a threat: let her go willingly at his word, or she will be taken by force, dragged by the hair. The threat sets up the next chapter, where Dhūmralocana is sent to do exactly that (6.3–4: केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम्).

Dragging by the hair is the extreme insult to a woman’s honour in the epic world. The threat turns back on those who make it: the asuras sent to seize her are destroyed, beginning with Dhūmralocana in the next chapter.

mantras.anvaya: एतत् एवम् (अस्ति): शुम्भः बली, निशुम्भः च अतिवीर्यवान्। किं करोमि? यत् मे प्रतिज्ञा पुरा अनालोचिता (कृता)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A concession (एवम् एतत्) spelled out in two nominal sentences; a deliberative question; a causal clause (यत् …) giving the reason.
mantras.lit: This is so: Śumbha is strong, and Niśumbha exceedingly valiant. What can I do, since my vow (was made) long ago without reflection?
mantras.tr: It is just as you say: Śumbha is mighty, and Niśumbha of surpassing valour. But what can I do? My vow was made long ago, without thought.

comm.t: The Devī concedes the messenger’s point about the brothers’ strength, as she did at first (5.118), and again pleads her old vow: she cannot set it aside. (A variant: for निशुम्भश्चातिवीर्यवान् the GRETIL Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and Freund read निशुम्भश्चापि तादृशः, the phrase of 5.118; the Gita Press reading is kept, and the sense is the same.)

The mock-helplessness (किं करोमि) and the claim that the vow was ill-considered (अनालोचिता) repeat the irony of 5.119. The vow cannot be broken, so the only way to her hand is through battle — which is the outcome she intends.

mantras.anvaya: सः त्वं गच्छ। मया ते यत् एतत् सर्वम् उक्तम्, तत् आदृतः (सन्) असुरेन्द्राय आचक्ष्व; सः च यत् युक्तं तत् करोतु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two imperatives addressed to the messenger (गच्छ, आचक्ष्व), the second with a relative pair (यत् … तत्) as its object; then a third-person imperative (करोतु) for Śumbha.
mantras.lit: So go, you; all this that has been said to you by me, report that with care to the lord of the asuras; and let him do that which is fitting.
mantras.tr: Go, then, and tell the lord of the asuras faithfully all that I have said to you; and let him do whatever he thinks fit.
mantras.tr_note: युक्तम् ‘what is fitting’ is rendered ‘whatever he thinks fit’, the usual sense of the formula.

comm.t: The Devī dismisses the messenger: he is to report her words exactly to Śumbha, and Śumbha must decide. The chapter ends here; the next opens with the messenger’s report and Śumbha’s anger (6.2–3).

The formula ‘let him do what is fitting’ courteously leaves the choice to the enemy, but the vow has already determined it: he can win her only in battle. In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter’s last mantra is followed by the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the recitation, not to the Purāṇa, and the colophon names the chapter देव्या दूतसंवादः, ‘the Devī’s dialogue with the messenger’.
